draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was their struggle a physical fight between living beings?"}
review: The proposed question is a reasonable first split, but it bundles two assumptions: that the struggle was physical and that both participants were living beings. A literal contest between objects could still fit the wording. Better ask: “Was their struggle a literal physical confrontation?” There is no visible history to rule out a repeated hypothesis.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was their struggle a literal physical confrontation?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Were Kameda and Umio competing in a game or contest with a goal other than avoiding physical damage?"}
review: The question is plausible, but it bundles “game or contest” and an assumed kind of objective. The only feedback so far rules out a literal physical confrontation; it does not establish that there was a formal competition. A more discriminating question: “Did observers judge who lost by a criterion other than the damage each sustained?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did observers judge who lost by a criterion other than the damage each sustained?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Were Kameda and Umio people?"}
review: “Were Kameda and Umio people?” is a reasonable broad discriminator, but the names alone don’t support assuming they were. The history rules out a literal physical confrontation and confirms observers used another criterion; it doesn’t establish what kind of entities or contest they were. No prior question has tested whether they were people, so this isn’t a repeat. You could submit it as written; avoid narrowing it to a specific contest or mechanism without more evidence.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Were Kameda and Umio people?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was their struggle a contest or competition, rather than a personal dispute?"}
review: The proposed question is plausible, but its contest-versus-personal-dispute framing is too narrow: the history only establishes that the struggle was nonliteral and that observers used another criterion. It could be an informal rivalry or another kind of conflict. A more discriminating question is: “Was success judged by whether either person achieved a defined objective, rather than by the damage they suffered?” This avoids assuming a formal competition or a particular scoring mechanism. No earlier question has directly tested that.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was success judged by whether either person achieved a defined objective, rather than by the damage they suffered?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Were Kameda and Umio competing in a sport or game?"}
review: The sports/game question is not already asked, but it assumes a contest format not established by the clues. A conventional game also often has a defined objective or result, and the answer to whether success was judged by achieving a defined objective was “no.” Better ask: “Was the non-damage criterion a subjective judgment rather than a formal result?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the non-damage criterion a subjective judgment rather than a formal result?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was their struggle a public argument or debate?"}
review: The debate/argument question is plausible but too specific: nothing in the history establishes that their struggle involved words or a public forum. The feedback only supports a nonphysical struggle, judged subjectively by a criterion other than damage; it rules out success at a defined objective. No earlier question repeats this hypothesis. Better discriminator: “Was their struggle part of a contest or performance that observers judged subjectively?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was their struggle part of a contest or performance that observers judged subjectively?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was their struggle a romantic relationship or breakup?"}
review: The romantic breakup angle is unsupported: the history establishes a nonphysical struggle and a subjective criterion, but rules out a contest/performance and an objective goal. It doesn’t identify a romantic context. Ask more broadly: “Did observers judge the loser by a social or emotional consequence of the conflict?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did observers judge the loser by a social or emotional consequence of the conflict?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was their struggle primarily a verbal argument?"}
review: The history does not rule out a verbal argument, but it doesn’t establish one either. “Primarily” also assumes a particular form of conflict. A more discriminating question is: “Did their struggle consist mainly of an exchange of words?” This tests the verbal-conflict hypothesis without treating it as fact. The clues so far support only that the struggle was nonliteral and that observers’ subjective judgment involved a social or emotional consequence.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did their struggle consist mainly of an exchange of words?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was their struggle a romantic or marital conflict?"}
review: The romantic/marital framing is unsupported: the history only establishes that observers used a subjective social or emotional consequence, not what kind. It also rules out a mainly verbal argument and a judged contest or performance. Ask a broader discriminating question: “Did observers think Umio suffered a greater social or emotional loss from the struggle, despite being physically unharmed?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did observers think Umio suffered a greater social or emotional loss from the struggle, despite being physically unharmed?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did observers think Umio was the loser because he felt guilt or remorse over what happened to Kameda?"}
review: The proposed question assumes Umio felt guilt or remorse; the feedback only establishes that observers thought he suffered a greater social or emotional loss. It does not say that loss was internal, or that Umio caused Kameda’s condition. A more discriminating question: “Did observers think Umio was blamed or judged negatively because of Kameda’s condition?” This tests a possible social consequence without treating it as established.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did observers think Umio was blamed or judged negatively because of Kameda’s condition?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was Kameda killed or left near death as a result of the struggle?"}
review:
The proposed question is too specific: “killed or left near death” assumes Kameda’s battered fragments describe literal bodily harm, despite the feedback that the struggle was not a literal physical confrontation. Nothing in the history establishes Kameda’s fate. It also combines two distinct possibilities. The history does establish a subjective social or emotional loss for Umio, but not its mechanism; observers did not think Umio was blamed for Kameda’s condition.

A more discriminating question: “Was Umio’s loss primarily emotional rather than social?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was Umio’s loss primarily emotional rather than social?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was Umio’s social loss that people saw him as cowardly or dishonorable for surviving the struggle unscathed?"}
review: The cowardice/dishonor theory is unsupported and likely conflicts with the earlier “no” to Umio being blamed or judged negatively because of Kameda’s condition. “Social loss” doesn’t establish that observers thought survival was shameful. A better discriminator: “Did Umio’s social loss involve losing a relationship or social connection with Kameda?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did Umio’s social loss involve losing a relationship or social connection with Kameda?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did observers think Umio had lost social standing or reputation as a result of the struggle?"}
review: The history supports a social consequence, but not its exact form: Umio’s loss was not primarily emotional, wasn’t loss of his connection with Kameda, and observers did not blame him for Kameda’s condition. Reputation is plausible, but the proposed wording narrows the explanation without support and may overlap with the rejected blame/judgment idea. A more discriminating question: “Was Umio’s social loss a concrete change in his circumstances, rather than a change in how others viewed him?” Don’t treat either answer as established yet.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was Umio’s social loss a concrete change in his circumstances, rather than a change in how others viewed him?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did Umio lose a job, position, or official role as a result of the struggle?"}
review: The job/position question is plausible, but it jumps from “a concrete change in his circumstances” to one specific kind of loss. Nothing in the history establishes employment or an official role. It does not repeat a rejected hypothesis: relationship loss, blame, emotional loss, and subjective contests have already been ruled out. A better discriminator is: **“Was Umio’s concrete loss imposed by an institution or authority?”** That tests a broad route to a circumstance change without presuming what he lost.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was Umio’s concrete loss imposed by an institution or authority?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did Umio lose a job, rank, or official position because of the struggle?"}
review: The proposed question jumps to a specific kind of loss—employment, rank, or office—that the history does not support. We know only that Umio suffered a concrete social loss imposed by an institution or authority. No earlier question has tested a job or position, so it is not a repeated hypothesis, but it is too narrow as the next step. Ask instead: “Was the authority’s action a direct consequence of the struggle, rather than an unrelated circumstance?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the authority’s action a direct consequence of the struggle, rather than an unrelated circumstance?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was Umio arrested or imprisoned as a result of the struggle?"}
review: The arrest/imprisonment proposal is too specific: the history only establishes that an authority imposed a concrete consequence directly because of the struggle, not that it was law enforcement or confinement. Ask instead: “Was the authority’s action a legal sanction?” This tests that broad category without presuming a particular mechanism. No prior question has already tested legal sanctions.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the authority’s action a legal sanction?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was Umio’s concrete loss that he lost his job or position? "}
review: The job/position hypothesis is plausible but unsupported: the history establishes a concrete, struggle-related loss imposed by an authority, not that Umio was employed or held a position. Ask a broader discriminator: “Did the authority remove Umio from an existing role or status?” This avoids assuming an employment mechanism while testing one possible form of the established loss.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority remove Umio from an existing role or status?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority impose a financial loss on Umio as a result of the struggle?"}
review: The proposed question is a reasonable discriminator: the history establishes an authority-imposed concrete consequence, but not what kind. Financial loss is unsupported so far, but the question tests it rather than assuming it. It does not repeat an earlier question; legal sanctions and removal from a role/status were already ruled out. No need to infer a particular mechanism from the mixed feedback.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority impose a financial loss on Umio as a result of the struggle?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority restrict Umio’s access to a place or activity because of the struggle?"}
review: This is a useful, not-yet-asked discriminator: the history establishes an authority-imposed concrete loss, but does not establish that it involved access. However, “a place or activity” bundles distinct possibilities and may steer toward one mechanism without support. Ask more broadly: “Did the authority restrict something Umio was allowed to do or access because of the struggle?” No prior question directly tests that. Don’t assume a ban, venue, or specific activity unless the answer confirms it.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority restrict something Umio was allowed to do or access because of the struggle?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did an authority deny Umio a specific opportunity or benefit because of the struggle?"}
review: The proposed question is too close to an already rejected hypothesis: the authority did not restrict anything Umio was allowed to do or access. Denying a specific opportunity or benefit is usually a form of that restriction, so a “yes” could muddy rather than clarify the story. The history also rules out a legal sanction, removal from a role, and financial loss; it does not identify what kind of institutional consequence occurred. A more discriminating question: “Did the authority require Umio to do something as a consequence of the struggle, rather than take something away?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority require Umio to do something as a consequence of the struggle?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority’s action cause Umio to lose something he possessed or valued, without directly restricting or requiring him to do anything?"}
review:
The proposed question assumes Umio lost something he possessed or valued; the history establishes only a concrete, authority-imposed loss. The “without restricting or requiring” clause mostly repeats already-rejected categories, and “possessed or valued” is broad enough to be hard to answer cleanly. The history also rules out a legal sanction, loss of role, financial loss, restriction, or required action, but does not identify what remained.

A more discriminating question: “Was Umio’s loss the loss of a future opportunity or benefit, rather than something he currently held?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was Umio’s loss the loss of a future opportunity or benefit, rather than something he already had?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did an authority take away or reassign something Umio already possessed, such as property or custody, because of the struggle?"}
review: The proposed question is plausible, but it bundles an unsupported mechanism—taking away or reassigning property or custody. The history establishes an authority-imposed concrete loss caused by the struggle, but does not establish what was lost. Earlier questions already ruled out losing a role/status, money, access, a required action, or a future benefit, so don’t simply revisit those. A cleaner discriminator: “Was Umio deprived of a specific possession he already had?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was Umio deprived of a specific possession he already had because of the struggle?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did Umio lose a family member or another important relationship with someone other than Kameda as a direct result of the struggle?"}
review: The proposed question is not a repeat: the earlier “no” ruled out losing a connection with Kameda, not with someone else. But asking about a family member or “important” relationship is a narrow mechanism not established by the history. A broader discriminator: “Did the authority’s action affect Umio’s circumstances through its effect on another person?” This tests the possibility without presuming the nature of the loss.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority’s action affect Umio’s circumstances through its effect on another person?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did an authority make Umio lose his home or place of residence as a direct result of the struggle?"}
review:
The home-loss hypothesis is unsupported, and it may overlap the earlier “restrict something Umio was allowed to do or access” question, which was answered no. The history establishes an authority-imposed, direct, concrete consequence, but rules out several familiar categories: legal sanction, role/status removal, financial loss, restriction, required action, lost future benefit, possession, and effects through another person. It does not point specifically to eviction.

A broader discriminator: **Did the authority’s action change Umio’s physical living conditions, rather than impose a sanction, duty, or loss of access or property?**
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority change Umio’s living conditions as a direct consequence of the struggle?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority cause Umio to lose or be denied a particular place, such as a home, seat, or position in a location?"}
review: The proposed question is poorly supported: losing or being denied a place overlaps the already-rejected idea that the authority restricted what Umio could do or access. “Position” also risks repeating the rejected removal-from-role hypothesis, and “home” overlaps the rejected change in living conditions. The history establishes an authority-imposed, direct, concrete change, but rules out many specific categories; it does not justify narrowing to a place. Ask instead: “Did the authority’s action change an official record or designation associated with Umio?” This probes a distinct possibility without treating it as established.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority’s action change an official record or designation associated with Umio?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority’s action cause Umio to lose a personal relationship with someone other than Kameda?"}
review:
The proposed question assumes a relationship loss, and that the authority’s action affected someone else. The history already says Umio did not lose a relationship with Kameda and the authority did not affect his circumstances through another person, so this is a poor next probe—even if it doesn’t strictly rule out every relationship involving someone else.

Repair: ask broadly, “What kind of concrete change did the authority impose on Umio?” That seeks the missing category without betting on another specific mechanism. Don’t treat the earlier yes/no answers as proof of any particular untested explanation.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority’s action change Umio’s physical or mental health?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority’s action affect Umio’s mental health rather than his physical health?"}
review: This is a useful follow-up, but “rather than his physical health” suggests the effects must be exclusive. The prior answer only says the authority changed Umio’s physical or mental health; it doesn’t rule out affecting both. Ask: “Did the authority’s action affect Umio’s mental health?” That cleanly tests one possibility without assuming the other. It is not a repeated question: the earlier question asked about health generally, and “Was Umio’s loss primarily emotional?” asked about the nature of his loss, not whether an institutional action affected his mental health.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority’s action affect Umio’s mental health?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority’s action cause Umio to become physically ill or injured?"}
review: The history supports that the authority’s action affected Umio’s health and that the effect was not mental, but it does not establish that he became ill or was injured. The proposed question bundles those possibilities and assumes a particular kind of physical effect. A cleaner discriminator is: “Did the authority’s action make Umio’s physical health worse?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority’s action make Umio’s physical health worse?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority worsen Umio’s physical health by subjecting him to a medical procedure or treatment because of the struggle?"}
review: The proposal is too specific: the history establishes that an authority’s action worsened Umio’s physical health, but nothing indicates a medical procedure or treatment. Also, the negative answers to questions about restrictions, requirements, and effects through another person do not identify the mechanism. Ask a broader discriminator instead: **“Did the authority’s action worsen Umio’s health by directly exposing him to a physical hazard?”** This tests one possible route without presenting treatment as established. The history has not already asked or rejected that question.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority’s action worsen Umio’s health by directly exposing him to a physical hazard?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority expose Umio to a dangerous environment as part of the struggle?"}
review: The proposed question is largely redundant: the history already confirms that an authority directly exposed Umio to a physical hazard, worsening his health as a consequence of the struggle. It doesn’t establish that the exposure happened “as part of” the struggle, so that phrasing may also assume a detail not yet supported. A more discriminating question would be: “Was the authority’s action directed specifically at Umio, rather than changing the situation in a way that exposed him to the hazard?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority deliberately expose Umio himself to the physical hazard?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the authority a medical or research institution that deliberately exposed Umio to a health hazard as part of a medical procedure or experiment?"}
review: The proposal adds two unsupported specifics: that the authority was medical or research-related, and that the exposure occurred during a procedure or experiment. The history only establishes that an authority deliberately exposed Umio to a hazard and that this worsened his physical health. Several broad alternatives have already been rejected (legal sanction, restriction, required action, and effects on another person), so don’t repackage those as a new guess. A more discriminating question would be: “Was the authority’s purpose in exposing Umio to the hazard to protect or treat someone, rather than to punish him?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the authority’s purpose in exposing Umio to the hazard to protect or treat someone, rather than to punish him?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was Umio sent by an authority into a war zone as a result of the struggle?"}
review: The war-zone question is too specific: the history establishes deliberate exposure to a physical hazard that worsened Umio’s health, but gives no evidence the hazard was warfare. The earlier “protect or treat rather than punish?” received “no,” which does not establish punishment; and “legal sanction?” received “no,” so avoid treating punishment as settled. A more discriminating question would be: “Was Umio’s exposure intended as punishment for his part in the struggle?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was Umio’s exposure intended as punishment for his part in the struggle?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was Umio deliberately exposed to the hazard as part of a scientific or medical experiment?"}
review: The experiment hypothesis is possible, but nothing in the history supports it over other reasons for deliberate exposure. The prior answers establish that an authority exposed Umio to a hazard, that this worsened his physical health, and that it was neither treatment/protection nor punishment; they do not identify the authority’s motive. Ask instead: “Was the authority trying to achieve a specific practical objective by exposing Umio?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the authority trying to achieve a specific practical objective by exposing Umio?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the physical hazard a toxic or radioactive substance?"}
review: The hazard itself is supported, but nothing in the history points specifically to a toxic or radioactive substance; that question bundles two guesses and narrows prematurely. The authority deliberately exposed Umio, but the feedback rules out punishment, protection/treatment, and a specific practical objective—not other reasons or contexts. A more discriminating question: “Was the exposure part of a general policy or procedure, rather than a decision aimed specifically at Umio?” This explores the authority’s role without presuming what the hazard was.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the exposure part of a general policy or procedure, rather than a decision aimed specifically at Umio?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the authority a government or military authority?"}
review: The government/military question is possible, but it only narrows the authority’s identity; nothing in the history supports either option. The history already rules out several tempting explanations: punishment, protection/treatment, a specific practical objective, or a general policy/procedure. Don’t infer one of those—or a particular authority—from “deliberately exposed.” A more discriminating question is: “Did the authority itself create the physical hazard?” This distinguishes creating the danger from exposing Umio to a pre-existing one without assuming what kind of authority was involved.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the authority itself create the physical hazard?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the physical hazard created by the authority a fire or explosion?"}
review: The fire/explosion question is possible but unsupportedly specific. The history establishes only that the authority created a physical hazard and deliberately exposed Umio; it does not point to fire or explosion. It also rules out punishment, protection/treatment, a specific practical objective, and a general policy/procedure, so avoid treating any of those as the explanation. A broader discriminator: “Was exposing Umio to the hazard itself the authority’s way of intervening in the struggle?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was exposing Umio to the hazard itself the authority’s way of intervening in the struggle?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the physical hazard radiation?"}
review: Radiation is possible but unsupported: the history establishes only that an authority deliberately exposed Umio to a physical hazard it created. It does not identify the hazard or suggest radiation in particular. No earlier question tested or rejected radiation, but the negatives about punishment, practical purpose, general policy, and intervening in the struggle do not point to it. Ask a broader discriminator first: “Was the hazard a substance or physical agent, rather than a dangerous condition or event?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the hazard a substance or physical agent, rather than a dangerous condition or event?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the physical agent a form of radiation?"}
review: Radiation is possible, but nothing in the history specifically points to it; the agent could be chemical, thermal, electrical, or something else. The proposal is a narrow guess, not an inference from the established facts. A more useful discriminator would be: “Was Umio exposed to the agent through inhalation or ingestion?” That tests a broad exposure route without presuming radiation. The history has already ruled out several explanations for the authority’s action—punishment, protection or treatment, a practical objective, general policy, and intervention in the struggle—so avoid reopening those.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was Umio exposed to the physical agent by inhaling it?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the physical hazard a weapon?"}
review: “Weapon” is an unsupported narrowing: the history establishes that an authority created a harmful physical agent and deliberately exposed Umio, but says the exposure was not punishment, protection/treatment, a practical objective, general policy, or intervention. No earlier question has tested whether it was a weapon, but the existing clues don’t imply one. Ask instead: “Was the agent harmful because of its inherent properties?” That distinguishes a hazardous agent from exposure to something ordinarily harmless without presuming a weapon or mechanism.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the agent harmful because of its inherent properties?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the harmful agent a chemical substance, such as poison, gas, or smoke?"}
review: The proposed question is too narrow: nothing in the feedback establishes a chemical, poison, gas, or smoke. We know only that the authority created a physical agent whose inherent properties were harmful; inhalation was irrelevant. Ask: “Was the harmful agent matter (a substance), rather than energy such as radiation or heat?” This separates broad possibilities without assuming a particular mechanism.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the harmful physical agent a material substance, rather than energy such as heat or radiation?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was Umio exposed to the harmful substance by ingesting it?"}
review: Ingestion has not been asked before, but it is a narrow mechanism with little support in the history. The prior inhalation question was marked irrelevant, which does not establish that inhalation did or did not occur; it suggests the route may not help solve the puzzle. A more discriminating question would connect the known facts: “Did Kameda’s condition cause or release the harmful substance to which the authority exposed Umio?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did Kameda’s condition cause or release the harmful substance to which the authority exposed Umio?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was Umio poisoned or otherwise made ill by the harmful substance?"}
review: The proposal is weak: physical-health worsening from deliberate exposure to a harmful material substance is already established, so “poisoned or otherwise made ill” largely repeats the known facts. “Poisoned” also introduces a specific mechanism not supported by the history, and the either/or wording may blur what a yes or no means. A more discriminating question would be: “Was the substance a chemical weapon?” That tests a distinct possibility without treating it as established.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the harmful substance a chemical weapon?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the authority’s deliberate exposure of Umio to the chemical weapon part of an experiment or test?"}
review: The experiment/test question is not contradicted, but it jumps to one specific motive. The history establishes deliberate exposure to a harmful chemical weapon, while rejecting punishment, protection/treatment, a practical objective, a general policy, and intervention in the struggle; it does not establish an experiment. No earlier question directly tested that hypothesis. A broader discriminator would be: “Was the authority’s exposure intended to harm Umio?” This tests an important unresolved point without presuming a particular mechanism.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the authority’s exposure of Umio to the chemical weapon intended to harm him?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the authority a military or government body?"}
review: The history supports an authority deliberately exposing Umio to a harmful chemical weapon, but it does not establish that the authority was military or governmental. That proposed question is a reasonable discriminator, though combining “military” and “government” could blur two distinct answers. Ask instead: “Was the authority a government body?” Don’t yet infer a war, deployment scenario, or motive: punishment, a practical objective, and general policy were all rejected. The story is not ready for a supported final explanation.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the authority a government body?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the authority a private organization or institution?"}
review: The proposed question is not repeated, and “Was the authority a government body?” was already answered no. But “private organization or institution” still assumes the non-government authority was an organization; the history doesn’t establish that. A cleaner discriminator is: **“Was the authority an individual rather than an organization?”** This distinguishes the broad remaining possibilities without guessing at the specific agent or motive, which the history has already explored extensively.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the authority an individual rather than an organization?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the authority that exposed Umio to the chemical weapon a criminal organization?"}
review: The proposed question is unsupported: nothing establishes that the non-governmental organization was criminal. The history has already established that the authority was an organization, not a government body or an individual, and that it intentionally exposed Umio to a harmful chemical weapon. It has not identified the organization’s legal status or motive beyond intending harm. No hypothesis in the proposal has already been asked or rejected, but “criminal” is an unjustified leap. A more discriminating question: “Was the organization itself a party to the struggle?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the organization itself a party to the struggle?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the organization that exposed Umio to the chemical weapon a criminal or terrorist group?"}
review: The proposal jumps to “criminal or terrorist” without support: we know only that a non-governmental organization, not itself a party to the struggle, deliberately exposed Umio to a chemical weapon to harm him. Ask a broader discriminator instead: “Was the organization primarily a military or armed organization?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the organization primarily a military or armed organization?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the organization that exposed Umio to the chemical weapon a terrorist or criminal organization?"}
review: The proposed question assumes a terrorist/criminal identity that the history does not establish. The organization deliberately exposed Umio to a chemical weapon, but that alone does not show it was terrorist or criminal; the answer that it was not primarily military was explicitly “irrelevant,” not evidence for another category. Nor should the mixed feedback be treated as proving a particular motive. A more discriminating question: “Was the organization responsible for arranging or authorizing the struggle?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the organization responsible for arranging or authorizing the struggle?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Were Kameda and Umio members of the organization that exposed Umio to the chemical weapon?"}
review: The membership question is possible, but the history doesn’t establish that either man belonged to the organization; it risks prematurely narrowing the story to an affiliation-based mechanism. The organization is known only to be a non-governmental, non-individual authority that was not itself a party to the struggle, and the weapon exposure was intended to harm Umio. A more discriminating question that doesn’t assume membership: “Was Umio targeted because of an affiliation or role unrelated to his personal involvement in the struggle?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was Umio targeted because of an affiliation or role unrelated to his personal involvement in the struggle?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the organization that exposed Umio to the chemical weapon a private company?"}
review:
The “private company” question is possible, but the history gives no support for that specific organization type. It also would not explain the key link: why an outside organization deliberately exposed Umio to a harmful chemical weapon as a consequence of the struggle. The history already rules out a government body, an individual, and the organization itself being a party; military status and arranging the struggle were marked irrelevant. No prior question directly tests the organization’s motive or connection to the conflict.

A more informative question would be: “Was the organization’s reason for targeting Umio connected to something that happened in the struggle?” This tests the missing causal link without assuming a particular kind of organization or motive.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the organization’s reason for targeting Umio connected to something that happened in the struggle?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the organization that exposed Umio to the chemical weapon a criminal organization?"}
review: The proposed question assumes the non-governmental organization is criminal; nothing in the history establishes that, and the weapon and intent to harm do not imply its status. A more discriminating question: “Was Umio targeted because of a specific action he took during the struggle?” This tests the established link to something that happened in the struggle without presuming what the organization was or why it acted.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was Umio targeted because of a specific action he took during the struggle?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was Umio targeted because he witnessed or learned something during the struggle?"}
